name: iced (iced-x86)
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, diStorm, udis86, BeaEngine (x86/x64 disassembler libraries); no GNU as, NASM or MASM assembler comparison
workload: Decode-only and decode+format of the 77 MB code section of Firefox's xul.dll (64-bit x86), single-threaded, MB/s of code bytes
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 256.69 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19, Zydis (min) 61.33, XED 55.39, bddisasm 35.48, diStorm 92.17 (about 7.5x Zydis and 4.6x XED, derived from page data). Decode+format: 149.21 MB/s vs Capstone 14.02, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, bddisasm 16.00, diStorm 58.85 (about 10.6x Capstone, 6.7x Zydis, derived from page data). iced README claim: 'Decodes >250 MB/s and decode+format >130 MB/s'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1 per README; flags from the repo build scripts (make-all.sh and bench/*/Makefile): C libraries built Release with -flto (XED --opt=3 -flto, diStorm bench -O3 -flto, Capstone bench -O3 -flto), Rust benches built with cargo build --release
hardware: Intel Core i5-6600K, Kubuntu 21.04 (README); test file xul.dll from Firefox 86.0.1.7739, 77 MB code section
tradeoffs: Rust library with an x86/x64 decoder, encoder, formatter and assembler; there is no official C or C++ API (bindings exist for .NET, Java, Python, JavaScript/WebAssembly and Lua), so use from C++ needs FFI or a wrapper. Decoded instruction is a 40-byte struct and the decoder does not allocate. x86/x64 only.
caveats: Benchmark lives in icedland/disas-bench, a fork of athre0z/disas-bench run by the iced authors, so it is not fully independent; the tables use 2021 hardware and toolchains and a single input file. The newer athre0z/disas-bench charts (Ryzen 9 9950X, i9-13900K, rustc 1.88/1.90, bars only, no numbers in the text) show iced still near the top but yaxpeax-x86 decode ahead of it. Disassembler baselines only: no comparison against GNU objdump/libopcodes, GNU as, NASM or MASM, and no assembling-speed measurement of iced's assembler.
found_via: WebSearch 'x86 decoder disassembler faster than Capstone Zydis XED benchmark github' surfaced the disas-bench harness; numbers read from the icedland/disas-bench README

name: yaxpeax-x86
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, diStorm (x86/x64 disassembler libraries); no GNU as, NASM or MASM comparison
workload: Decode-only and decode+format of the 77 MB code section of Firefox's xul.dll (64-bit x86) in the disas-bench harness
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 182.08 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19, XED 55.39, bddisasm 35.48, diStorm 92.17 (about 5.3x Zydis, 3.3x XED, derived from page data). Decode+format: 40.05 MB/s vs Capstone 14.02, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, bddisasm 16.00 (about 2.9x Capstone, derived from page data). Repo README claim: 'roughly 250mb/s decode throughput and on some hardware is the fastest software x86 decoder available', 'an average of 58 cycles on a zen2 core'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1 per README; flags from the repo build scripts (make-all.sh and bench/*/Makefile): C libraries built Release with -flto (XED --opt=3 -flto, diStorm bench -O3 -flto, Capstone bench -O3 -flto), Rust benches built with cargo build --release
hardware: Intel Core i5-6600K, Kubuntu 21.04 (README); test file xul.dll from Firefox 86.0.1.7739, 77 MB code section
tradeoffs: Rust crate (part of the yaxpeax project), no C API, so C++ use needs FFI; about 143 kB of code and data for the decoder (249 kB with formatting). x86 only in this crate.
caveats: Harness is third-party (athre0z/iced fork) but the README tables list yaxpeax below iced in decode-only (182.08 vs 256.69 MB/s) and below iced and diStorm in decode+format (40.05 vs 149.21 and 58.85). The README's 250 MB/s and 58 cycles on zen2 figures come from the author's own runs and are not on the benchmark page. The newer athre0z/disas-bench Ryzen 9 9950X bar chart (unlabelled, read by eye) puts yaxpeax decode at roughly 460 MB/s, ahead of iced at roughly 360 MB/s; no text numbers to quote. The author calls the crate's in-repo benchmark 'so unrealistic as to be unuseful' and prefers disas-bench.
found_via: WebSearch 'x86 decoder disassembler faster than Capstone Zydis XED benchmark github' surfaced disas-bench; yaxpeax-x86 README links to it; numbers read from the icedland/disas-bench README

name: diStorm3
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, udis86, BeaEngine (x86/AMD64 disassembler libraries); no GNU as, NASM or MASM comparison
workload: Decode-only and decode+format of the 77 MB code section of Firefox's xul.dll (64-bit x86) in the disas-bench harness
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 92.17 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19, XED 55.39, bddisasm 35.48, udis86 80.72 (about 2.7x Zydis, 1.7x XED, derived from page data). Decode+format: 58.85 MB/s vs Capstone 14.02, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, bddisasm 16.00 (about 4.2x Capstone, 2.6x Zydis, derived from page data). README: 'ultra fast', and quotes a 2014 thesis that benchmarked five open-source disassembly libraries and chose diStorm3 for best performance.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1 per README; flags from the repo build scripts (make-all.sh and bench/*/Makefile): C libraries built Release with -flto (XED --opt=3 -flto, diStorm bench -O3 -flto, Capstone bench -O3 -flto), Rust benches built with cargo build --release
hardware: Intel Core i5-6600K, Kubuntu 21.04 (README); test file xul.dll from Firefox 86.0.1.7739, 77 MB code section
tradeoffs: C library with a single decompose API (returns a structured description, optional text formatting), about 45 KB, x86/AMD64 only; Python bindings (distorm3). No commits since 2021 (date read from the GitHub commits page), so recent instruction-set extensions are unlikely to decode.
caveats: Benchmark is third-party but the iced authors' fork, 2021 hardware and toolchains, single input file. diStorm trails iced (92.17 vs 256.69 MB/s decode-only) and yaxpeax-x86 in decode-only, but is second in decode+format. Disassembler baselines only; nothing against GNU objdump/libopcodes. The README quote of the 2014 thesis is a testimonial, not a measurement on the page.
found_via: WebSearch 'objdump alternative faster than GNU objdump disassembly' and the disas-bench results; numbers read from the icedland/disas-bench README

name: Zydis
baseline: Capstone, Intel XED, bddisasm, BeaEngine, udis86 (x86/x64 disassembler libraries); no GNU as, NASM or MASM comparison
workload: Decode+format and decode-only of the 77 MB code section of Firefox's xul.dll (64-bit x86) in the disas-bench harness
claimed_speedup: Decode+format: Zydis 22.24 MB/s vs Capstone 14.02, XED 15.67, bddisasm 16.00, BeaEngine 13.42, udis86 12.02 (about 1.6x Capstone, derived from page data). Decode only: Zydis (min) 61.33 MB/s vs XED 55.39 and bddisasm 35.48; full Zydis 34.19 MB/s. Zydis README only says 'Optimized for high performance'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1 per README; flags from the repo build scripts (make-all.sh and bench/*/Makefile): C libraries built Release with -flto (XED --opt=3 -flto, diStorm bench -O3 -flto, Capstone bench -O3 -flto), Rust benches built with cargo build --release; Zydis built with CMake Release and -flto
hardware: Intel Core i5-6600K, Kubuntu 21.04 (README); test file xul.dll from Firefox 86.0.1.7739, 77 MB code section
tradeoffs: C99/C11 library with no dynamic allocation and a C API, directly callable from C++; also has an encoder/code-generation API. The 'min' decode mode drops most operand data, which is why it is faster than the full mode.
caveats: Win over Capstone is modest (1.6x decode+format) and Zydis loses to iced, diStorm and yaxpeax-x86 in the same tables (full decode-only 34.19 MB/s vs XED 55.39 and diStorm 92.17). Listed as the widely used incumbent with a measured advantage over Capstone, not as the fastest. Benchmark is the iced authors' fork on 2021 hardware; Zydis's own README has no numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'x86 decoder disassembler faster than Capstone Zydis XED benchmark github' (disas-bench); numbers read from the icedland/disas-bench README

name: aron
baseline: macOS as (Apple's system assembler, not GNU as)
workload: Assembling one test file, test.macos.s, comparing assemble time against macOS `as`
claimed_speedup: 'aron is 12.94 ± 2.34 times faster than as' (text is the alt text of the README benchmark image)
tradeoffs: Incomplete x86-64 assembler: only ELF64 and Mach-O output, a subset of the instruction set, Rust crate used as a command-line tool, not a library.
caveats: Author writes 'This is not empirical by any means'; single input file, no hardware, flags or run count stated, benchmark image only (the 12.94x figure is alt text). Baseline is macOS as, not GNU as or NASM. Speed on a tiny input may be dominated by process start-up (inference). Because the assembler is incomplete, the work done differs from a full assembler.
found_via: WebSearch 'assembler assembles million lines per second fast two-pass assembler github benchmark vs GNU as' and a second 'Show HN x86-64 assembler written from scratch faster than GNU as' query

name: minias
baseline: GNU as and the clang (LLVM integrated) assembler
workload: Assembling AT&T x86-64 assembly emitted by GCC, Clang, cproc/QBE and chibicc into relocatable ELF objects (no specific workload given)
claimed_speedup: 'performance is often better than gnu as and much better than the clang assembler' (README Notes; no numbers)
compiler_and_flags: Builds with cc -O2 (README build commands); no benchmark flags
tradeoffs: Supports a practical subset of AT&T x86-64 only; ELF relocatable output; not a library; deliberately omits many GNU as extensions and does not free memory (OS reclaims). Parser is generated by Minipeg from a PEG grammar and is the stated speed limiter.
caveats: Only evidence is one README sentence with no numbers, versions, machine or workload; included as the single tier D entry because it names GNU as and the clang assembler directly. Author lists simple immediate expressions and a full opcode test matrix as unfinished roadmap items.
found_via: WebSearch 'assembler assembles million lines per second fast two-pass assembler github benchmark vs GNU as'

name: B2R2 disassembler
baseline: Capstone (Capstone.NET and Capstone Python bindings), plus SharpDisasm; compared with iced (C#), which is faster
workload: Seconds to disassemble three raw binary blobs (blob_x86, blob_x86_64, libc_x86 from the BAR19-Artifact repo), average of 10 runs
claimed_speedup: B2R2 28.298 s on blob_x86, 24.317 s on blob_x86_64, 0.63 s on libc_x86 (average 17.748 s) vs Capstone.NET 127.847 / 106.414 / 2.245 s (average 78.835 s) and Capstone Python 132.693 / 111.604 / 2.22 s (average 82.172 s): about 4.4x faster than Capstone.NET on average (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: .NET release mode (dotnet run -c release) per tool; B2R2 v0.5.0; Capstone Python run through a script
tradeoffs: Fully managed F# binary analysis framework (also lifts to IR and recovers CFGs, not measured here); needs .NET, no C or C++ API, so use from C++ requires interop or a separate process.
caveats: First-party comparison by the B2R2 authors; no CPU, OS or compiler flags stated; the DisasmComparison repo has no stated licence and its last commit is 2021-10-23 (benchmark repo stale). Baseline is Capstone through .NET and Python bindings, not native Capstone, so marshalling overhead probably inflates the gap. In the same table Iced (C#) is faster than B2R2 (average 15.737 s vs 17.748 s).
found_via: WebSearch 'objdump alternative faster than GNU objdump disassembly binutils replacement benchmark github' surfaced B2R2-org/DisasmComparison
